questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement between coders
questions.learningObjective: Explain why raw agreement percentages mislead about coder reliability.
questions.stem: A moth-trapping team wants to know whether two coders agree beyond chance on a shared transcript. Explain why a raw agreement percentage is not enough.

answer.exemplar: Two coders can agree on nearly everything by chance if the code list is short and the categories are unbalanced, because most segments then receive the most common code. Chance-corrected agreement, such as Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha for more than two coders, compares observed agreement with the agreement expected from the marginal distribution of codes. Reporting the correction alongside the raw figure shows whether the coders are genuinely aligned rather than merely following the frequency of the dominant code.

questions.explanation: Raw agreement can be inflated by chance when codes are few or unbalanced, so a corrected statistic shows whether coders genuinely align. The raw percentage hides how much the code distribution gives.
questions.hint: Agreement must be compared against what chance gives.

questions.learningObjective: Compute coding coverage across two overlapping coding schemes.
questions.stem: In a rocky shore survey, the team codes 210 transcript excerpts. A fixed codebook covers 165 excerpts and emergent codes cover 90, with 45 excerpts carrying both a codebook and an emergent code. How many excerpts carry at least one kind of code?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Unequal sample sizes across mixed phases
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unequal phase sizes limit combined analytic claims.
questions.stem: A survey combines a small intensive phase with a large extensive phase. Explain how unequal sample sizes affect what the combined analysis can claim.

answer.exemplar: When one phase contributes far more observations than the other, the pooled analysis is dominated by the larger phase, and any theme it contains will look more prevalent simply because it had more chances to appear. The two phases therefore need separate denominators, so prevalence is reported within each phase before the results are compared. Conclusions can then say that a theme is concentrated in the intensive phase, or widespread in the extensive phase, which a single pooled percentage would conceal.

questions.explanation: Pooling phases with unequal sample sizes lets the larger phase dominate, making its themes look prevalent by weight of numbers. Reporting each phase against its own denominator preserves contrasts.
questions.hint: Give each phase its own denominator.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Discarding singleton codes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequence of discarding singleton codes.
questions.stem: A marsh invertebrate survey produces 60 codes, 22 of which appear only once. Explain what happens if those 22 codes are discarded and what that costs.

answer.exemplar: Discarding the 22 singleton codes leaves 38 codes carrying the substance of the corpus, and it can sharpen the analysis by removing categories that rest on a single passage. The cost is that a singleton is not necessarily an error: it may mark a genuinely rare but meaningful event, such as one sighting of a protected species or one description of unusual behaviour. Good practice is to record why each singleton was dropped, so the decision is auditable rather than silent, and to keep a list of the discarded codes for later audit.

questions.explanation: Discarding singletons trims the codebook of categories resting on one passage, but it removes rare meaningful material. Recording the rationale makes the choice auditable.
questions.hint: Rare is not the same as wrong.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Codebook versus emergent coding in thematic analysis
questions.learningObjective: Compare the gains and risks of codebook and emergent coding.
questions.stem: A rodent survey team must choose between a fixed codebook and free coding. Explain what each approach gains and what it risks.

answer.exemplar: A fixed codebook gives every interview the same analytic frame, so findings can be compared across sites, counts mean the same thing throughout, and a second coder can be checked against the same reference. Its risk is that categories which the protocol never imagined will not appear in the findings, and what participants actually emphasise can be squeezed into an ill-fitting slot. Free coding keeps the material's own structure intact and surfaces unanticipated concerns, but it produces categories that are local to one analyst and one transcript.

questions.explanation: A fixed codebook buys comparability but can force material into ill-fitting slots. Free coding surfaces unanticipated concerns but yields categories local to one analyst, so prevalence stays weak.
questions.hint: Comparability against openness.

questions.stem: A lichen survey team wants to report how common a theme is across interviews. Explain what a good prevalence statement must specify.

answer.exemplar: A defensible prevalence statement names the theme as it was defined in the analysis, states the number of interviews in which it appears, and gives the denominator as the interviews actually coded, with a note on any excluded material. questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Deductive and inductive codes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a hybrid analysis produces and the problem it creates.
questions.stem: Protocol codes and codes built from transcripts are combined in this survey. Explain what a hybrid analysis looks like and what problem it creates.

answer.exemplar: In a hybrid analysis the deductive layer is applied first, so every interview is coded against the categories the protocol specifies. Reading the coded material then shows where those categories fail, and inductive codes are added for what the frame could not hold. The analytical problem is that the two layers now sit at different levels of confidence, and the analyst must decide how to report them: a theme that appears only in emergent codes may be important and thinly evidenced, while a theme visible in both layers is better supported.

questions.explanation: A hybrid analysis applies the deductive layer, then adds inductive codes where the frame falls short, producing layers of unequal support. The analyst must report that difference.
questions.hint: Two layers, unequal support.

questions.topic: How widespread a theme is across interviews
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for establishing that a theme is widespread.
questions.stem: In an upland survey, which sequence best describes how a team should establish that a theme is widespread across the interviews?

options.text: Fix the definition, count interviews where it appears, report the denominator and caveats, then note gaps.
Count the interviews where it appears, then adjust the definition until the count matches the claim.
options.misconception: Adjusts the definition to fit a preferred claim

options.text: Ask every interviewee whether the theme applies to their site, then report the proportion who agree.
options.misconception: Uses self-reported applicability instead of coded evidence

options.text: Search the transcripts for the theme's key word, count the hits, and report that count as its prevalence.
options.misconception: Counts word hits as a measure of thematic prevalence

questions.explanation: Widespreadness rests on a fixed definition, a count of interviews where the theme appears, a denominator, and a report of absences. Adjusting the definition to fit a claim produces a chosen number.
questions.hint: Define, count, divide, and note absences.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Share of talk time in a focus group
questions.learningObjective: Compute a participant's share of participant talk time in a session.

stimulus.body: Focus group on reserve access, four participants, 50 minutes recorded. Participant A speaks for 19 minutes, B for 13, C for 9, D for 4, and there is a further 5 minutes of moderator questions and 0 minutes of silence between turns.

questions.stem: The focus group tally above records participant contributions. Which statement about participant A's contribution is correct?

options.text: A speaks for 19 of 45 minutes of talk, which is about 42 percent, the largest single share of the floor.
A speaks for 19 of 50 minutes of session, which is 38 percent, the largest single share of the floor.
options.misconception: Uses the session length including moderator turns

options.text: A speaks for 19 of 45 minutes of talk, which is about 42 percent, and this proves A dominated the group.
options.misconception: Turns a high share into a conclusion about group dynamics

options.text: A speaks for 19 of 54 minutes of talk, which is about 35 percent, the largest single share of the floor.
options.misconception: Adds silence that the record shows was absent

questions.explanation: Participant talk time totals 45 minutes once the moderator's five are excluded, so A holds 19 of 45, about 42 percent. That makes A the largest voice, a fact about airtime rather than about the group.
questions.hint: Exclude moderator time before dividing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Unequal sample sizes across mixed phases
questions.learningObjective: Compare theme prevalence across phases with their own denominators.
questions.stem: A survey has 15 interviews in phase A and 45 in phase B, with a theme in 3 and 27 interviews respectively. First state which phase shows the theme as more prevalent, then give the phase B percentage.

options.text: Phase B shows the theme as more prevalent, at 60 percent against 20 percent in phase A.
Phase A shows the theme as more prevalent, at 60 percent against 20 percent in phase B.
options.misconception: Reverses the phase comparison

options.text: Both phases are equally prevalent, because 30 of 60 interviews carry the theme, which is 50 percent.
options.misconception: Pools the phases and calls equal prevalence the result

options.text: Phase B shows the theme as more prevalent, but its share is 27 of 60, which is 45 percent.
options.misconception: Uses the pooled denominator for one phase's rate

questions.explanation: Phase B has the theme in 27 of 45 interviews, 60 percent, against 3 of 15 in phase A, 20 percent, so it is markedly more prevalent in phase B. Pooling gives 30 of 60, describing neither.
questions.hint: Percentages need their own phase denominators.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Codebook versus emergent coding in thematic analysis
questions.learningObjective: Compute the excerpts left uncovered by two coding layers.
questions.stem: A survey codes 300 excerpts, of which 180 fit the fixed codebook and 140 are covered by emergent codes, with 50 in both groups. How many excerpts are covered by neither scheme?
questions.explanation: The union is 180 plus 140 minus 50, which is 270, so 30 of the 300 excerpts carry neither code. Those 30 matter because a prevalence figure over the union covers only the coded part.
questions.hint: Union first, then the gap to the corpus.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Deductive and inductive codes
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps for generating inductive codes.
questions.stem: For a wetland survey, which sequence best describes how inductive codes should be generated from interview material?

options.text: Read it without a fixed frame, mark meanings as they appear, compare across interviews, then name them.
Apply the protocol codes first, then read the material again and rename the protocol categories to fit.
options.misconception: Renames existing categories instead of generating new ones

options.text: Write down every possible category before reading, then assign each excerpt to the closest category.
options.misconception: Pre-specifies categories before reading the material

options.text: Search the transcripts for the survey's key terms, then count how often each term appears in each interview.
options.misconception: Counts term frequency and calls it inductive coding

questions.explanation: Inductive coding starts by reading without a fixed frame, marking meanings as they appear and comparing them across interviews before naming them. Renaming protocol categories imposes a scheme.
questions.hint: No frame, mark, compare, then name.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement between coders
questions.learningObjective: Read raw and chance-corrected agreement figures together.

stimulus.body: Two coders on the salt-marsh interview. Agreement on 82 of 96 excerpts, 80 percent raw. Code distribution for both coders: GRAZING 40, RESTING 18, MIGRATING 8, AVOIDANCE 6, FORAGING 12, plus four codes used once or twice. Chance-corrected value for this transcript: 0.58.

questions.stem: The agreement summary below reports results from a salt-marsh interview. Which reading of these figures is correct?

options.text: Raw agreement is 80 percent and the corrected value is 0.58, which is above chance but below strong agreement.
Raw agreement is 82 percent and the corrected value is 0.58, so the corrected figure is the weaker of the two.
options.misconception: Reports a match count as a percentage

options.text: Raw agreement is 80 percent and the corrected value is 0.58, so coders should stop because it is acceptable.
options.misconception: Treats a moderate agreement value as a stopping point

options.text: Raw agreement is 80 percent and the corrected value is 0.58, so small code counts make it unreliable.
options.misconception: Dismisses the corrected value for unsupported reasons

questions.explanation: Eighty-two of 96 excerpts is about 80 percent raw, and a corrected value of 0.58 shows agreement beyond chance but short of strong reliability, so the coding frame needs checking.
questions.hint: Compare the corrected value against chance, not perfection.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Discarding singleton codes
questions.learningObjective: Define a singleton code and count the codes used more than once.
questions.stem: A survey codes 250 excerpts and creates 90 codes, of which 25 appear in only one excerpt. First state what a singleton is, then give the number of codes used more than once.

options.text: A singleton is a code applied to one excerpt only, and 65 of the 90 codes are used more than once.
A singleton is a code applied to one interview only, and 65 of the 90 codes are used more than once.
options.misconception: Defines the unit as the interview rather than the excerpt

options.text: A singleton is a code applied to one excerpt only, and 90 of the 90 codes are used more than once.
options.misconception: Ignores the singleton codes when counting the rest

options.text: A singleton is a code applied to several excerpts in an interview, and 25 of 90 codes are used more than once.
options.misconception: Reverses the meaning of singleton and miscounts 25

questions.explanation: A singleton is a code attached to exactly one excerpt, so with 25 of 90 in that position the remaining 65 are each used more than once. That count describes the codebook's support.
questions.hint: One excerpt is the unit for a singleton.
